newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire war more a rout than a rumble in the jungle.
newsitem.headline: Zaire war more a rout than a rumble in the jungle.

text.p: Battlefields are hard to find and body-counts scarce in Zaire's civil war, but allegiances shift day by day from the government to the rebels, and so Laurent Kabila's revolt advances.

There were two swollen corpses still lying in the grass at Lubumbashi airport on Sunday, and the usual scattered detritus of spilled bullets, flattened badges, discarded uniforms and family snapshots that might have denoted a battle, or a rout.
But there were no scorch marks on the walls, no shell craters, no burnt-out vehicles; just four or five isolated bullet holes in the plate-glass doors.
An ancient, Egyptian-made heavy machinegun stood abandoned in front of the arrivals hall.
This was where the feared presidential guard of Marshall Mobutu Sese Seko might have made a stand a few days ago against Kabila's rebel army, before yielding to superior force.

Or maybe not. There have been unconfirmed reports that the guard fled by air back to Kinshasa, and some villagers have reported seeing retreating units in the bush between here and the Zambian border.

Ask a rebel officer in French what happened, and he plainly does not speak the lingua franca of Zaire. Perhaps he is from Rwanda, or Uganda, as has been reported of this force. It is difficult to pin down.

He is driving the white and blue pickup of a major local trucking company, whether requisitioned or donated is unclear. But one thing at least is sure: in areas now firmly under Kabila control, big business is talking to the rebels.
In this newly "captured" city, everyone who is anyone has already jumped on the Kabila bandwagon.
Anyone closely linked to Mobutu's repressive apparatus, and who failed to hedge his bets in the final days, appears to have fled.
Kabila may have timed his challenge to Mobutu perfectly, instead of resisting the uprising, the 32-year-old regime collapses under a rolling wave of peoples' power.

In Lubumbashi, Zaire's second city, scarcely a window was broken when rebels took over last week. Seven people were shot for looting and there was an undetermined number of casualties in fighting around the town. The army went over to Kabila.
But the rebel leader has still not arrived here to hold his by now customary victory rally and to consolidate his support.
The city is on tenterhooks, anxious to see what kind of administration will emerge from the election process they expect.

An opposition politician said:"We don't want this revolution against the Mobutu regime to be stolen from us by opportunists who cleverly switch sides to ride on Kabila's coat tails. We want change, and true democracy. New revolution, new men."
Among Lubumbashi expatriates, some smile cynically at what they regard as a pious hope.
Six months after beginning his rebellion in the east, Kabila has risen from total obscurity and now controls half of this vast country, about the size of western Europe.
More to the point perhaps, in a land with few roads, he occupies the half that makes the money, from mineral deposits of diamonds, gold, copper, cobalt and tin.

But miners make less than 100 dollars a month and many sites lay unexploited or in miserable disrepair, the result of the rulers' "kleptocracy", which siphoned off hard currency profits to the capital, Kinshasa.
The countryside of potentially rich Shaba province has the mudhuts, thatched roofs and potholed roads of abject poverty and state neglect.
